analysis.one_liner: Orders a government study of how drug middlemen's price-linked fees and payment structures work.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with bipartisan sponsorship and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat with no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directs the Comptroller General, the head of Congress's investigative agency (the GAO), to study how the many middlemen in the prescription drug supply chain pay each other based on a drug's price — including pharmacy benefit managers, insurers, wholesalers, pharmacies, drug makers, and rebate-processing firms. It specifically looks at whether fees set as a percentage of a drug's price give these companies a financial reason to favor more expensive drugs, and it requires a report to Congress with recommendations within two years of enactment.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the main beneficiaries would be consumers and employers who pay for prescriptions, because a detailed public accounting of price-linked fees — and of the conflicts of interest they create — would give lawmakers the evidence needed to reform pharmacy benefit manager practices. Congress and federal health agencies would also gain a clearer map of who takes what cut along the supply chain. The GAO would receive a new, funded mandate.

how_it_helps.text: Requires an independent federal study of how much and in what ways intermediaries in the drug supply chain — pharmacy benefit managers, Part D plan sponsors, wholesalers, pharmacies, manufacturers, rebate aggregators, and consultants — are compensated based on a drug's price, including the pricing benchmarks they use [S2].

Directs the study to examine conflicts of interest, specifically whether fees calculated as a percentage of a drug's price favor selecting, distributing, or purchasing higher-priced drugs — the mechanism by which middlemen's fees can raise costs for patients and health plans [S2].

Requires the study to compare how affiliated companies (those with common ownership or subsidiary relationships) versus unaffiliated companies structure these payments, which would shed light on vertical consolidation in the drug supply chain [S2].

Requires the Comptroller General to report results and recommendations for legislative and administrative action to Congress within two years of enactment, giving lawmakers a evidence base for reform [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The direct costs are minimal: taxpayers would fund the GAO study, which is a routine federal expense. The real exposure falls on pharmacy benefit managers, rebate aggregators, wholesalers, and consultants, whose price-linked fee structures would face public scrutiny and potentially become the basis for future regulation that could reduce their revenue. Consumers and patients would bear the ongoing cost of the status quo in the meantime, since a study delivers no price relief on its own.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug middlemen facing scrutiny of their fees

drawbacks.text: The bill produces only a study and a report; it changes no pricing practice, caps no fee, and delivers no direct relief to patients paying high drug prices, with the report due no earlier than two years after enactment [S2].
Its findings would be non-binding — the Comptroller General can only recommend legislation and administrative action, so even a damning report does not require Congress to act [S2].

The GAO has already examined pharmacy benefit manager compensation and conflicts of interest in prior work, so this study may partly duplicate existing government analysis rather than uncover new information.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a low-cost, low-risk transparency step: it would arm Congress with a comprehensive map of price-linked fees and their conflicts of interest across the entire drug supply chain, at essentially the price of one federal study. But it is deliberately modest — two years of waiting, no binding rules, and no guarantee anyone acts on the recommendations. It is a precursor to reform, not reform itself.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has not been taken up, and Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Senator Michael Bennet introduced the bill in the Senate on January 29, 2026, joined by Republican Senator James Lankford [S1].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day [S4].
No further action has been taken on the bill since its referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody yet, because nothing has happened — though pharmacy benefit managers and other supply chain intermediaries are better off for now, since scrutiny of their fee structures remains confined to a stalled bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug supply chain middlemen, for now

for.name: Sen. Michael Bennet
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill directing a GAO study of price-related compensation in the prescription drug supply chain.

for.name: Sen. James Lankford
for.what_they_did: Joined Bennet in introducing the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from the start.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and has taken no action on it since January 29, 2026.

sides.party_line_note: The bill is bipartisan in origin — a Democrat introduced it with one Republican cosponsor — and no votes or committee action have yet revealed whether broader support or opposition splits by party.

industries.note: PBMs are the first-named subject of the study. The bill targets the core of their business model — fees calculated as a percentage of a drug's price, which the bill itself notes can favor higher-priced drugs — so a rigorous public accounting threatens their current compensation structures.

Rebate aggregators, brokers, auditors, and consultants who advise plan sponsors on PBM contracts are explicitly included in the study's scope, subjecting their slice of price-linked payments to public scrutiny for the first time in one consolidated review.

Wholesalers and pharmacies are part of the payment structures under study, which could expose practices that squeeze independent pharmacies; their interest in the bill's findings is genuinely two-sided.

Manufacturers are included in the study of price-based compensation, and findings on how supply chain fees inflate net prices could build support for broader pricing reforms that manufacturers oppose.
Plan sponsors are subjects of the study and also, as payers, potential beneficiaries of any reform that curbs PBM fees; the bill's effect on them depends on what the findings are used to do.

analysis.trajectory: Most GAO-study bills never reach the Senate floor, and this one has sat untouched in the Finance Committee since referral. Its realistic path is attachment as a provision to a larger, must-pass package — such as PBM reform legislation or Medicare extenders — rather than standalone action; otherwise it will expire when this Congress ends.
